newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Some Slovak banks fail to meet reserve reqs - NBS.
newsitem.headline: Some Slovak banks fail to meet reserve reqs - NBS.

text.p: Some Slovak banks on Wednesday failed to fulfil their minimum reserve requirements, the first time this has happened in the country's banking sector, official figures from the central bank (NBS) showed.

According to NBS figures published in a statement, the sector as a whole was short of liquidity as of the minimum reserve deadline on Wednesday, with banks' filling only 97.75 percent of their minimum reserve requirements.

NBS officials would not comment on which banks failed to meet the requirements, but local analysts said they estimated three to six banks, possibly including some of the market's reference banks, were included on the list.
The minimum reserve requirement for January is set at 34.231 billion crowns. Local banks submit a balance sheet for assessment to the central bank each fortnight.

Banks must have liquid reserves to cover nine percent of time and demand deposits. If banks fail to meet minimum reserve demands they must pay a penalty of three times the country's discount rate, which currently stands at 8.8 percent.

The interbank market has faced an acute liquidity shortage since the NBS stopped quoting securities repo and reverse repo rates. It has opted instead to hold tenders on a daily basis, if needed, for limited volumes of short-term securities repurchases.
Earlier on Wednesday the NBS held a one-day repo tender offering three billion crowns of liquidity, but it was undersubscribed with bids for only 2.88 billion crowns.

"We offered the sector in this morning's tender less liquidity than it needed and the tender was still undersubscribed, which could be due to shortened interbank credit lines that the current illiquidity crunch has brought about," said Peter Andresic, head of the NBS open market operation department.
The NBS has said that by reducing refinancing volumes, it hopes to help curb credit expansion which is at the heart of the country's burgeoning money supply.
